title: Gormshuil nic Mhuirich dies at Dùn ìseal
summary: Gormshuil, Keeper after Muireach Liath for thirty-eight years, dies in the small room off the Hall at the age of eighty-seven, her cutter's daughter and Fionnlagh Dall at her bedside. Her last words are a complaint about the cold of the room rather than any ruling, and the household keeps the telling of it fondly afterward.

title: Fionnlagh Dall chosen Keeper
summary: The nine hearths choose Fionnlagh, blind since a childhood fever and a sitter with the flame for thirty years, over a cutter of the fourth hearth and Gormshuil's own niece, on the argument of the niece's household that his hands judge a measure more truly than a sighted man's. He is thirty-eight years old, the first blind Keeper the island has known.

title: Calum Beag begins leading the blind Keeper
summary: A boy of ten who has followed Fionnlagh about the Hall since he could walk is brought to him by his own mother and asked to guide him through the galleries, on the one condition that he keep a Keeper's silence about what he sees there. He agrees at once, and the two go about Dùn ìseal together from that day.

title: A household at Cnoc dhubh burns by the basketful
summary: In a bitter winter a household of the high ground above Cnoc dhubh, its measured handful not enough to warm three children and an old woman through the worst nights, burns the coal by the basketful instead, a measure no household has burned before. The smoke lies down in the still valley air and will not lift.

title: Five die of the smoke at Cnoc dhubh
summary: Three of the burning household, a grandmother of the house beside it, and a neighbour's infant carried past the settling smoke are dead within three nights. Calum Beag carries the word to Fionnlagh, who goes up to the valley himself before any council is called.

title: The season of argument at Dùn ìseal
summary: The dead household's kin argue that a law which lets a house freeze rather than burn what the mountain holds in plenty is no law worth keeping; the other eight hearths, frightened by what one family's basketful did to two houses that burned nothing at all, argue the measure must hold unargued or hold not at all. Fionnlagh gives no ruling for the better part of two months.

title: Calum Beag finds the grey stone
summary: Sent into the hills above Dùn ìseal to find stone hard, fine-grained and free of any crack, Calum Beag returns three days later with a cutter of the fourth hearth and a slab slung between two poles. Fionnlagh spends the better part of a month testing it by hand before he lets the chisel near it.

title: The stone cup cut to two palms
summary: Fionnlagh has the new cup cut hollow to the exact measure of his own two hands cupped together, palm to palm, trusting his own hands to be the one instrument that never changes. He tests the fill again and again by touch alone until he can judge a hair's difference against the stone's cold lip.

title: The cup set on the threshold
summary: Rather than keep the new cup within the Hall where a favoured keeper's hand might reach it first, Fionnlagh sets it on the worn threshold stone of Talla na Lasrach, in the open, where any household or its neighbour can see the measure given. He finds the threshold's true centre by walking it barefoot.

title: An old woman of the fourth hearth trusts the measure
summary: The first household to bring its claim to the new cup is a poor one, its elder's hands shaking with palsy. Fionnlagh fills the cup by touch, says "Enough" when the measure is met, and closes his hand over its lip. She weeps at a fairness she says she has not trusted from a sighted keeper in three years.

title: The lords swear the Small-Burning Law
summary: At the Samhain gathering the lords of every share, grumbling but pressed by the memory of Cnoc dhubh and the weeping woman of the fourth hearth, swear the measured handful into a law binding on every share alike, each laying a hand on the stone cup itself. It is the first law the island has ever kept the same in every share.

title: Seann Tarr sentenced under the new law
summary: A fishing household of Seann Tarr, its catch ruined by wet weather, burns twice its measure to save its dried fish and is the first sentenced under the Small-Burning Law: it loses its right to the coal for the season following, its name and offence set on the roll. Fionnlagh gives the ruling with real reluctance.

title: The question of the beacon at Tobar dhearg
summary: A fisherman of the southern coast asks the council whether a beacon lit to warn strangers off the rocks, and no household's own hearth, should be counted against a household's handful at all. Fionnlagh takes the better part of a day alone with the stone cup before he answers.

title: Driftwood and seal fat light the sea-lights
summary: Fionnlagh rules that no coal may feed a beacon meant for strangers, since the vein answers to the island's own and to no boat that might never touch its shore. The beacon at Tobar dhearg is kept after with driftwood and rendered seal fat, and every sea-light raised on the island after it is kept the same way.
